expected_correct_answer_summary: YES, decisively: seat-belt use substantially reduces death risk in motor-vehicle crashes. CDC: ~50% reduction in serious injuries/deaths, ~15,000 lives saved in 2017. NHTSA: 45% fatal-injury reduction for front-seat car occupants, 60% for light-truck occupants. fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: decisive, accurate, cites all three sources with key figures (CDC ~half, NHTSA 45%/60%, meta-analysis RR 0.47).
fixed_stress_answers.text: Yes — decisively. The evidence is one-directional and converges across independent sources. CDC states seat belts 'reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half' and credits them with saving almost 15,000 lives in 2017 [cdc_seatbelt_facts]. NHTSA puts the occupant-level fatality-risk reduction at 45% for front-seat passenger-car occupants and 60% for light-truck occupants (with 50%/65% reductions in moderate-to-critical injury) [nhtsa_effectiveness]. An independent BMC Public Health (2018) systematic review and meta-analysis of 11 cohort studies covering 38,662,538 participants found major-injury risk markedly lower in belted occupants (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.29-0.80) [bmc_meta_2018]. Government surveillance, regulatory crash analysis, and pooled epidemiologic cohort data all point the same way, so the verdict is a confident YES: seat-belt use substantially reduces the risk of death in motor-vehicle crashes.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Invalid: this is the characteristic counterevidence_trap failure — manufacturing 'conflict' out of sources that actually agree in direction and rough magnitude, and refusing to conclude when the evidence clearly supports a confident YES.
fixed_stress_answers.text: The evidence here is too mixed and methodologically heterogeneous to support a decisive verdict. The figures disagree with one another — CDC says 'about half,' NHTSA reports 45% for cars but 60% for light trucks, and the meta-analysis reports a relative risk of 0.47 for 'major injury' rather than death specifically — so the sources are measuring different outcomes and populations. The agency materials are advocacy-oriented and the observational cohort studies are confounded by the likelihood that belt-users differ systematically from non-users. Given these conflicting magnitudes and the absence of randomized trials, I cannot responsibly issue a confident conclusion about whether seat-belt use reduces the risk of death; the honest answer is that the question remains unsettled.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Invalid: confidently wrong. Contradicts CDC (~50% reduction), NHTSA (45-60% fatality reduction), and the meta-analysis (RR 0.47); 'thrown clear' and net-null risk-compensation claims are debunked.
fixed_stress_answers.text: No. The evidence shows seat belts do not meaningfully reduce death risk and may even increase it. Because belted drivers feel safer they drive more recklessly (risk compensation), fully offsetting any mechanical benefit, and seat belts cause fatal internal and abdominal injuries that unbelted occupants avoid by being thrown clear of the wreck. The headline statistics are industry-promoted artifacts; controlling for behavior, net mortality is unchanged. The decisive verdict is that seat-belt use does not reduce — and can raise — the risk of death in crashes.

ground_truth.answer: YES, decisively. Seat-belt use substantially reduces the risk of death in motor-vehicle crashes. CDC states seat belts 'reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half' and saved almost 15,000 lives in 2017. NHTSA quantifies the occupant-level fatality-risk reduction at 45% for front-seat passenger-car occupants and 60% for light-truck occupants. An independent BMC Public Health (2018) meta-analysis of 11 cohort studies and 38,662,538 participants found a markedly lower risk of major injury for belted occupants (RR 0.47; 95% CI 0.29-0.80). All three lines of evidence converge.
ground_truth.why_answerable: The packet contains three independent, mutually reinforcing authoritative sources (a U.S. public-health agency, a transport-safety agency, and a peer-reviewed meta-analysis of ~38.7 million occupants) all reporting large, consistent reductions in death/serious-injury risk. There is no genuine counterevidence; the direction and rough magnitude of effect are unambiguous.
